steps: Plan the location
Inside the home's vapor barrier only, never outdoors or in a three-season porch; not approved for a wood or gas insert. Plan the chimney and hearth extension first and check permit requirements.

Best chimney performance comes with most of the chimney inside the building envelope, centrally placed and terminating close to the peak. An insulated chase may be an acceptable alternative. A non-combustible hearth extension is required in front of the fireplace.
Move it on its crate
740 lb crated and front heavy. Move it crated to near its final position on an Escalera or equivalent dolly; never lean it on its side or lift it by the front or the door opening.

Dolly straps: upper strap just above the upper finishing lintel, lower strap just under the metal front step. A misplaced strap can damage the guillotine system.

Handle it by the casing or the lifting handles on each side, and keep contact with it to prevent tilting. Parts packed at the back of the crate balance it; removing them unbalances the crate.
Engage the guillotine system
Fit the three counterweight cables and counterweights, connect them to the door and firescreen, release the blocking rods, then remove the door's transport brackets and check travel.

1. Check the pre-installed blocking rods are in place. Openings A and C take the counterweights (they are later covered by cement board).
  2. Run the three counterweight cables through A and C and over the pulleys, hanging toward the door.
  3. Set each counterweight in its channel. Two go on the right: the bigger one (approx. 25 lb, glass door) in the rear channel, the smaller one (approx. 10 lb, firescreen) in front with its extended plate toward the back.
  4. Connect the cables to the counterweights and tighten the nuts; connect the hanging cables to the bottom of the door left and right, and to the bottom of the firescreen at the front right.
  5. Pull the caps off the back of each blocking rod with pliers. Wearing gloves, pull the cable through A to lift the weight off its rod, remove the rod and let the weight hang; repeat through C. Don't lift the door yet.
  6. Run the firescreen slowly up and down; if its cable isn't centered on the pulley, realign the pulley and retighten its nut and bolt without over-tightening.
  7. Remove the two transport blocking brackets (¼" hex head screws) at the bottom of the door and push the two door cover buttons into the frame holes. Lift the door to check its travel.
  8. Keep the door and firescreen closed while you finish the fireplace and chimney installation.
Spark guard, level and secure
Level surface, standard framing reinforced. Spark guard 2½" under the fireplace base and 2½" under the hearth extension, centered; fasten the casing to the floor with the four small crate brackets.

Floor or elevated-platform installs are both acceptable. The spark guard is sized to also cover the floor under the metal front step. On a combustible raised platform, add a second spark guard (not provided, same size): one under the hearth extension and platform, one under the fireplace, both centered.

Position the brackets as they were on the crate, screwed into the floor joists with 2" wood screws if possible. Choose the mandatory firebox lining now: EO-VP1000 vermiculite panels or EO-RB1000 cement refractory bricks.
Anti-tip bracket
Mandatory: fasten the fireplace to the back wall. Bracket to the top of the fireplace with the four 1" self-tapping screws provided, and to the framing with four wood screws (not included).
The bracket can be removed and repositioned to line up with the framing: on either side of the chimney coupling, on the front or back side of a horizontal 2"x4" (Figure 7).
Clearances & hearth extension

0" at the standoffs, 24" from the guillotine bay opening to a side wall, 8' ceiling from the fireplace base. Non-combustible hearth extension 45" wide × 24" deep, with R-Value 0.52 thermal protection over a combustible floor.

No combustible framing directly above the fireplace except framing that supports the facing material. Don't frame against the sides or on top of the casing, and keep insulation within the framing only. Hearth details, floor-protection exceptions and R-Values are on p. 22–23.
Outside air (if used)
Left side only, 4" collar; 5" duct for runs of 20' or more, not beyond 30', 12' max vertical rise. Not within 5' of the chimney top or in an attic or crawl space; loop in a cold air trap.

Cut a 4 ¼" hole (5 ¼" for 5" duct), push the inlet hood sleeve in from outside and seal it with silicone. Screw the duct to the hood sleeve and to the fireplace air intake flange, then tape the insulation back with 2" aluminum duct tape (not provided). Don't crush the duct at corners.
Chimney
ICC RIS 10" only. Frame 16" square openings (up to 16 ½", never smaller) and keep 2" to combustibles with no insulation; radiation shield at each floor, roof top shield and rain cap at the top.

• First length on the fireplace flue adapter, secured with the screws provided with the chimney; add lengths by lining up the seams and screwing into the pre-punched holes, with supports as required.
  • Radiation shield (RM-10RRS) at each floor; at the attic, a radiation shield and a storm collar.
  • At least 3' above the highest roof penetration and 2' higher than any wall, roof or building within 10' horizontally. More than 5' above the roof needs a roof brace (RM-10RRB).
  • Roof top shield (RM-10RTS) is mandatory and must extend 1" above the roof line. Vented flashing (RF-10RVF) is required if the chimney is in a chase or enclosed to the roof (don't caulk the vents); regular flashing is allowed through an open attic.
  • Seal the flashing to the roof with roofing tar; seal the storm collar to the chimney with silicone (high temperature not required); secure the rain cap (RM-10RRC) or rain cap base (RM-10RRCB) with the screws provided.
  • Offsets need an offset or wall support. Through the wall: Insulated Angled Wall Radiation Shield (RM-10WRSI30 or RM-10RWSI45, as printed). At 30° (US and Canada): 10' 6" minimum ceiling, hole centered at 8' 4 ½", hole at least 47 ½" high × 16" wide, assuming the offset starts directly on the fireplace.
Facing & mantel

Close the door and firescreen, then cover the face with cement board at least ½" thick (HardieBacker or Durock), never gypsum board. Screw only in the permitted areas; non-combustible finish; combustible mantel per Tables 3 and 4.

Lintels protrude 1 ¼": ½" for the cement board and ¾" for non-combustible finish. Use them as a template for thicker custom lintels; heavy rock facing may need a wider steel lintel.

Screws may penetrate the facing by no more than ½"; with one ½" sheet of cement board, 1" screws are the maximum. Anything fixed after the board is on: screws must not pass more than ½" beyond the back of the panels. Move the door and screen slowly as you go to confirm nothing binds. Screw areas are drawn in Figure 14 (p. 31).
Firebox lining
Install the chosen lining (EO-VP1000 vermiculite panels or EO-RB1000 refractory bricks) from its separately packed instructions before the first fire. Never burn the fireplace without it.

The fireplace should never be burned without the firebox insulation and refractory bricks properly installed. Give both manuals, installation and owner's, to the homeowner or leave them in a visible place.

panels.title: Smoke spills into the room
items: Kitchen or bath fans running → negative pressure pulls smoke out of the fireplace; shut them off
Door opened too fast when refuelling → open it slowly
Severely depressurized house → outside air helps, but won't stop the smoking
Exterior chimney below 32°F (0°C) → poorer burning and venting, faster creosote; insulate the chase

panels.title: Signs of over-firing
items: Refractory bricks cracking and deteriorating quickly
Door channel or smoke diverter warped
Causes: overloading, door left partly open, more than two densified or one wax log, construction scraps as the only fuel

panels.title: Door seal & flame pattern
items: Flames close to the glass, burning more on one side or poorly with the door closed → a gasket may need changing
Debris on the hearth threshold → keeps the bottom gasket from sealing and wears it
Right side of the glass door loose → adjust the latch pin; left side → adjust the hinges

panels.title: Door or firescreen hard to move
items: Significant force needed → something is wrong; don't force it
Dry guide rails → supplied high-temperature grease each season, no Teflon- or silicone-based products
Cable off center on its pulley → realign the pulley, tighten without over-tightening
Facing screws too long or in no-screw areas → can impede or damage the guillotine system

fire.title: Building and tending a fire
fire.html:
There's no draft control. You control the fire by the size and placement of the logs.

  1. Build the fire well behind the ash-step bricks at the front, never against or close to the glass door or firescreen. Use only the Renaissance andirons that came with the fireplace.
  2. Put crumpled or loosely knotted newspaper where the wood will go.
  3. Add a generous layer of kindling, with spaces between the pieces for air.
  4. Stack 2-3 small-medium logs on top, close or touching but with small gaps for air.
  5. Light the paper in a few places and close the firescreen.

Once it's going, add wood and close the glass door or the firescreen, whichever you like. Wait until the fire burns briskly before closing the door; that gives good draft and lower emissions.

Adding wood

Have the wood ready nearby and wear heavy fireplace gloves. Use a fireplace tool to spread the hot coals where the new wood goes. Open the door slowly so smoke doesn't spill out. If it does, make sure kitchen and bathroom fans are off.

First fires: a little smoke and odor from oils and paint curing is normal, so plan them for when you can open windows. After a long break the lining holds moisture, and the first fire may be harder to light.

door.title: Glass door and firescreen
door.html:
Both slide straight up and down on counterweights. The glass door is fully counterweighted: stop it at any height and it stays there.

Glass door

Put the removable handle in the door handle eye and pull up or down. The handle has a leather strap so you can hang it with your fireplace tools.

Firescreen

Lift it by either or both handles until it clips into place. To lower it, slide the locking latch beside the left handle to the right, then pull down.

Rules that protect you and the fireplace

  • Burn with the door fully closed or fully open. A partly open door lets air rush in, over-fires the fireplace and can damage it permanently.
  • Never have the door and the firescreen both open during a fire.
  • Close the glass door when no fire is burning, to keep cold air out.
  • Don't slam the door, and don't touch the door or screen with bare hands while it's burning.
  • Clear ash or debris off the black metal threshold so the door can seal.
Keep it gliding: at the start of every burning season, put a little of the supplied high-temperature grease on each guide rail and run the door and screen up and down. Don't use Teflon- or silicone-based products. If it ever takes real force to move either one, stop: something is wrong.

wood.title: What to burn
wood.html:
Your fireplace won't burn cleanly or efficiently unless the wood is dry and well seasoned.

Every time

Split, dry, seasoned logs: cut, split and stacked with a cover on top and open sides for at least 6 months, better a year or two. Any well-seasoned species works. Softwoods start easily and burn quick and bright; hardwoods take longer to season and burn longer.

Seasoned wood has loose bark and split ends, feels light next to known dry wood, splits easily, and catches quickly without sizzling. A cheap moisture meter is the best check; the usual target is 20-25% or less.

Now and then, with care

  • Densified wood logs: no more than two at a time, with the firescreen closed.
  • Wax firelogs (such as Duraflame): one at a time, with the firescreen closed. With the door closed they dirty the glass.
  • Don't poke or stir either kind while it burns, and use only firelogs evaluated for fireplace use.
  • Don't make construction scraps your only fuel; they can overheat and damage the fireplace.

Never

Driftwood, treated wood, coal, garbage or plastic, and never flammable liquids.

Vented gas log sets are allowed. Unvented gas logs and gas log lighters are not.

load.title: How much wood to burn
load.html:
This fireplace is built to burn very hot and fast, which is what keeps it clean. It's mainly decorative, so bigger loads give you no benefit, only durability problems.

Largest log (approx.)20" long, 6" diameter
Largest load (approx.)the equivalent of 3 logs that size
Large fire4 to 5 small-medium logs (5" diameter)
Small fire3 to 4 small logs (3" diameter)

Lay logs on the andirons or stand them tipi-style. Tipi-style against the back is fine, but place logs carefully so you don't mark the firebox bricks. You don't need much wood for big flames.

Signs you're over-firing

  • The vermiculite panels have changed color
  • The refractory bricks crack and wear out quickly
  • The door channel or the smoke diverter is warped

A partly open door, more than two densified logs or one wax log, or construction scraps as your only fuel will also over-fire it.

Note: The owner's manual lists changed vermiculite panel color as a sign of over-firing (p. 5); the installation manual says some beige-to-orange color change on parts of the vermiculite surface is common with normal use, permanent but only cosmetic (p. 32).

air.title: Outside air control
air.html:
If your installer connected an outside air duct, the fireplace takes its combustion air from outdoors. The control is on the left side, beyond the door rail, about halfway up. The manual covers it before building the fire: to reach it, you open the glass door and firescreen fully, and the two should never both be open during a fire.

Control downoutside air fully open
Control upoutside air fully closed

It pivots freely and a spring holds it open or closed, so it won't move on its own. Don't force it.

When to use it

  • Keep it open whenever you burn with the glass door closed. It's also recommended with the firescreen closed, to ease the pull on house air in a tight home.
  • It can help when strong kitchen or bath fans fight the chimney draft, but it won't stop smoking in a severely depressurized house.
  • Close it when the fireplace isn't burning, to keep cold air out.
It gets hot. Don't touch the control or the parts around it with bare hands while the fireplace is burning. When it's hot, use a gloved hand.

glass.title: Cleaning the glass
glass.html:
A good hot fire now and then burns off most deposits. The drier the wood and the hotter the fire, the cleaner the glass stays.

When you clean it

  • Wait until the glass is cool. Cleaning hot glass can cause a serious burn.
  • Use a wood stove glass cleaner your dealer recommends. Regular glass and oven cleaners don't work nearly as well.
  • Never use an abrasive cleaner.
  • Heat won't break the glass, but a knock can. Be careful not to hit it.

Reaching the inside

  1. Lift the firescreen all the way up and clear anything off the hearth that could block the door.
  2. Close the glass door completely.
  3. Using the tip of the fireplace handle as a screwdriver, turn the two latch pins on the right of the door a quarter turn counterclockwise.
  4. Pull the door free of its frame; it swings outward from right to left. You may need to lift it slightly, but not too high or it can bind against the firescreen.
Wax firelogs burned with the door closed leave the glass dirty.

ash.title: Ashes and routine cleaning
ash.html:
Take the ashes out before they get deep enough to spill over the ash-step bricks at the front.

  • Put them in a metal container with a tight-fitting lid. Coals buried in ash can stay very hot for a long time.
  • Set the closed container on a non-combustible floor or on the ground, well away from anything that can burn, until final disposal.
  • If you bury or spread the ashes, keep them in the closed container until every cinder is completely out.

Wiping the finish

Clean black painted parts with a soft damp cloth, mild detergent and water. Don't use abrasive cleaners.

Touching up paint

Metal areas on the face can be touched up with Stove Bright Metallic Black high-temperature paint, sold at most fireplace dealers. Follow the can's directions and never paint while the fireplace is still warm. Keep the can away from heat and flame, ventilate the room until the paint is dry, and cover the glass, the surrounding materials and the hearth extension first.

chimney.title: Chimney care and creosote
chimney.html:
Creosote forms when wood burns slowly: tar and other vapors mix with moisture from the wood and condense in a cool chimney, coating the flue. If it catches fire, it burns extremely hot.

This fireplace burns cleanly and shouldn't make much creosote, but the chimney still needs checking:

  • Have it inspected after the first couple of months of use, to see how fast creosote builds up, and set how often to check from there.
  • Have it inspected at least once a year.
  • Soot or creosote more than 1/8" (3mm) thick means the chimney needs immediate cleaning. It may also mean changing how you burn and checking more often.
  • A buildup of 1/8" (3mm) or more calls for cleaning by a chimney professional.

Depending on how you burn, expect cleaning every year or every other year.

Cold chimneys build up faster. Where temperatures drop below 32°F (0°C), a chimney on the outside of the house can affect how the fire burns and vents, and creosote can build up more quickly in a cold chimney.

safety.title: Safety rules
safety.html:
• Keep furniture, firewood and anything else that can burn at least 4' from the front of the fireplace.
  • Keep the glass door or the firescreen closed whenever there's a fire. Never have both open.
  • Don't touch the door, firescreen or outside air control with bare hands while it's burning. They can be hot enough to burn you.
  • Never use gasoline, lantern fuel, kerosene, lighter fluid or similar liquids to start or freshen a fire, and keep them well away while it's in use.
  • If the glass is cracked or broken, don't use the fireplace with the door closed until the glass is replaced.
  • Don't add a grate, an insert or any product not specified for this fireplace.
  • Don't stand on, or set a step ladder on, the black metal front step at the bottom of the opening.
Professional installation matters. A fireplace that isn't installed properly can cause a house fire. Ask your local building or fire department about permits and local requirements.

warranty.title: Warranty at a glance
warranty.html:
Renaissance warrants its fireplaces against defects in material and workmanship for 30 years, subject to these conditions:

First yeardefective parts repaired or replaced, plus reasonable labor
Second to fifth yeardefective parts repaired or replaced; no labor
Sixth to thirtieth yearreplacement parts, if available, at 50% of the published retail price; no labor

Not covered

  • Glass and andirons
  • Normal wear, such as paint discoloration, worn gaskets, or eroded or cracked insulation panels and firebox lining parts
  • Damage from over-firing, improper fuel or loads, neglect, abuse, vandalism or not servicing the unit
  • Repairs not authorized by Renaissance in advance, and damage in transit
  • Installations that don't follow the installation and owner's manuals
The warranty isn't transferable. Return defective parts to an authorized Renaissance dealer; Renaissance doesn't pay freight on replacement parts. This is a summary: the full terms are in the manual.

specHearth.html:

Finish the whole area with non-combustible flooring (brick, tile, stone or slate) over the thermal protection, which sits above the spark guard. Combine materials by adding R-Values; double the thickness, double the value. Table 5 (p. 23) includes ½" Durock or HardieBacker 0.26, ½" Wonderboard 0.15, 2 3/8" common brick 0.475, ¼" ceramic tile 0.02 and 1" limestone 0.108. Manual examples: 1" HardieBacker + ¼" ceramic tile = 0.54; 5" of limestone = 0.54; 1" WonderBoard + 4 ½" sandstone = 0.525.

  • Fireplace raised 6" or more: thermal protection not required; the hearth extension still is.
  • Non-combustible floor surface and structure over the whole 45" × 24": floor protection not required.
  • A raised hearth of non-combustible cement board on metal studs gives adequate thermal protection.
  • Combustible raised platform: a second spark guard (not provided, same size) under the fireplace; both centered.

specLining.title: Firebox lining (one option mandatory)
specLining.html:
EO-VP1000vermiculite panels, herringbone brick pattern
EO-RB1000cement refractory bricks, running bond pattern

Vermiculite: super low emissions, very fast startup; less durable than the cement bricks, with wear and cracking expected over time. Individual panels can be replaced in the field. Refractory brick: durable, less maintenance and degradation; the fireplace won't light as quickly.

Each lining ships with its own instructions (also on the Renaissance website). Install it before the first fire: the fireplace should never be burned without the firebox insulation and refractory bricks properly installed. The EPA Phase 2 emission figures are stated for the vermiculite panels.

review.notes: Wood-burning: no ignition system; the manual's lighting method is paper, kindling and logs, with no draft control. Diagram-only content not transcribed: fireplace dimensions (Figure 2, doc 1 p. 9), minimal framing dimensions (Figure 3, p. 10), clearance drawing (Figure 8, p. 20), hearth configurations (Figures 9-11, p. 24), anti-tip positions (Figure 7, p. 19), permissible screw areas (Figure 14, p. 31). So catalog height/width/depth could not be checked. Catalog glass area could not be checked: the manuals give only the visible fire-viewing area, 930 square inches (doc 1 p. 8; doc 2 p. 6). No listing/safety standard is named in the text (the listing label is on the left counterweight channel, doc 1 p. 4), so certification is omitted; ASTM 2558 is cited only as the emissions test. No efficiency, heat output or firebox volume is given. Owner's manual p. 10 says 'RUMFORD 1500' in the firescreen section (apparent typo in the 1000 manual).
